role: Analysis module: compares 7200 with 8000 MT/s rates, writes FACTS.md sections 4 to 6
purpose: The file defines the function `section4`, which writes sections 4, 5 and 6 of the facts sheet `FACTS.md` and the Q2 entries of the verdict object of `facts.json`. The function compares the rates in GB/s of the 7200 MT/s rerun with the rates of the earlier 8000 MT/s runs, by the rules that were fixed before the run.

main_flow.step: The module imports helper functions and fixed texts from `facts_data.py` and `facts_text.py`, and it sets two labels for the rows F72d12 and control I. It has no command line and it does no work when it is imported. `facts_text.py` calls `section4` once, after it has written the title lines, the heading of section 0 and sections 1 to 3. It writes the text of section 0 after the call [Ref1].
The function `secs` is defined. It prints the interval lengths of a record list, for example `6 s`.

`section4` starts. It takes the collected data `D`, the statistics `N`, the verdict object `V`, the list of output lines `L`, the reference function `ref`, the row writer `q2row` and the context `c`. It unpacks the record lists and the comparisons that `facts_text.py` prepared, for example `L72o`, `P12o` and `cLo`.

Four local helpers are defined: `src` (reference labels of the csv files of a record list), `ranges` (a table with one min-to-max range per row), `source` (the Source cell of the row table) and `cmps` (the table of the overlap tests, which also stores each test for `facts.json`).

One description text per earlier row is set (`DESC`). The three argument lines like.spec, cfwd.spec and crev.spec are read. The build stops unless they differ only in the value of `--seq` and row L-1 ran the line of like.spec.

Section 4.1, rules and rows. The rule summary is written. The build stops unless rows A-1 to A-3, L-1 to L-4, R0, R0b, B7a, B7b, C3a, C3b, B5a and B5b share one boot label and every 7200 MT/s record holds the boot id of try6.txt. The second part of this check tests no file of the run. `build_facts.py` copies the boot id of try6.txt into every 7200 MT/s record [Ref3]. Rows X2d12, X1d10, X1d10b and BASEd10 are 8000 MT/s rows of other boots, and this check leaves them out. It also leaves out rows B5a-rev and B5b-rev, which come from the same two folders as B5a and B5b. A table of the 22 earlier rows is written: binary, stop rule, memory speed, load at launch, number of interval records and processes. Then the proof is written that row F72d12 ran in the boot of the rerun. The build stops unless the F72d12 process lies between two readings of the same boot id: try6.txt before it and the first state line of go.sh after it.

Section 4.1, hardware error records. For the processes of rows L-1 to L-4, R0 and R0b the table says where each error record of the saved journal lies against the intervals that the sheet uses (oldread at position 0 and asmread at position 1 of each round). The build stops unless two records of one second lie inside the lowest asmread interval of the pool L-1 to L-4. The pool without this interval is stored as `P12a_wo` for section 4.4.

Section 4.1, hypothesis on corrected records. For every interval to which records can be assigned the table gives its rate minus the rate of the same kernel at the same position in the other round of the same process. Records at the border of two intervals cannot be assigned to one interval. The text counts them, and their intervals are not in the table. A difference counts when it is above `LIM` = 1.0 GB/s. The text says what fits the hypothesis and what does not.

Section 4.2, old read kernel, parts A and L. Part A: the range of `bw_old read` of the rerun (`A72o`) is tested against rows A-1, A-2, A-3 and their pool (`A80o`). Part L: the range of oldread (`L72o`) is tested against L-1 alone, the pool L-1 to L-4 (`P12o`) and the pool with R0 and R0b (`PALLo`). The oldread ranges of F72d12 (`F72o`) and of control I (`I72o`) are tested against the same three record lists. For part L the distance of the nearest ends, of the medians and of the farthest ends is computed in GB/s and in percent.

Section 4.2, view by start state. The processes of the pool L-1 to L-4 are split into two groups by the 1-minute load average at launch: below 1.0 (`idle`), or 1.0 and above (`busy`). The build stops unless every `busy` process was launched at most 30 s after a 120-thread bwx12 process ended. The oldread and asmread ranges of each group are formed. Parts L and C are compared with the second group. A group of the same kind is formed from the bwx11 rows: the processes that were launched at most 30 s after a 120-thread bwx11 process ended. For rows B7a, B7b, C3a and C3b of runner bwx the code takes every process and checks that it follows a 120-thread step in its csv file. It checks no time limit there.

Section 4.2, old read kernel, part C. The oldread intervals of part C (`C72o`) are tested as one list. They are also tested separately by position: position 0 (cfwd) and position 2 (crev, directly after read).

Section 4.3, new read kernel in part A (rule V3). For each cell of `pa3` (binary, load-only kernel, round) the three intervals of session 1 get the wording inside or outside the 8000 MT/s range of the same round. One entry per cell is added to `V['q2_rows']`. The medians of `bw_new read` in session 1, row A-1 and row A-2 are compared.
Section 4.3, view at an equal pass count. The same cells are compared again with only the intervals that completed 663 or 664 passes.

Section 4.3, thread rates. The sum of the thread rates of an interval is estimated as 120 x the column `per_thread_avg_GBps`. The distance of the nearest ends by this estimate is set next to the distance by `aggregate_GBps`. The estimate is checked against the per-thread rows of A1.csv.

Section 4.4, asmread in part L. The asmread ranges of part L (`L72a`), F72d12 and control I are tested against L-1 alone, the pool L-1 to L-4 (`P12a`) and the pool with R0 and R0b (`PALLa`). The tests are repeated against the pool without the interval that holds the error records.

Section 4.5, load-only kernels in part C, grouped by the kernel that ran directly before. Kernel `read` has no bwx12 run at 8000 MT/s. Its two groups are shown next to the rows of runner bwx and get no wording. The group "asmread after oldread" is tested against the pool L-1 to L-4.

Section 4.6, the three visits of the like.spec line in the 7200 MT/s boot (F72d12, part L, control I). The build stops unless the three asmread ranges lie in rising order without overlap: F72d12 lowest, then control I, then part L. The spread between the lowest and the highest value is computed. The distances of part L to F72d12 and to the pool L-1 to L-4 are stored in `c['dist']`. The texts that rule V1 points 3 and 4 require are written from the 10-module rows.

Section 4.7, sums per mesh. For each row the lowest and the highest value of `mesh0_GBps` and of `mesh1_GBps` are printed. The build stops unless oldread at 7200 MT/s gave more on mesh 1 and less on mesh 0 than the bwx12 and bwx11 rows at 8000 MT/s.
Section 4.8, a table that is kept as a record: the lowest to highest total of read_nop96, read_nop256 and read_1pl in part L, control I, F72d12 and L-1. No statement is made from it.

Section 4.9, verdict for Q2. Two verdict texts are built from the values above: `V['q2_old_read']` and `V['q2_new_read']`. They are joined as `V['q2']`. Three more objects are stored for `facts.json`: `same_boot`, `pool_8000_by_start_state` and `part_A_thread_rates`.
Section 5, a table that is kept as a record: write, copy, asmwrite and asmcopy of part A. A cell holds n, the lowest, the median and the highest rate. No statement is made from it.

Section 6, three lists: what is established, what is not established (`V['insufficient_data']`) and the hypotheses H1 to H5 (`V['hypotheses']`). Before the lists are built, the build stops unless every integrity check of `build_facts.py` passed (line 1461) [Ref3]. The code counts in how many load-only cells of part A the round-2 process lies above the round-1 process without overlap. Here a cell is one session with one of `bw_new read`, `bw_old asmread` and `bw_new asmread`. That gives 9 cells.

behavior_notes: Where a rate comes from. This file reads no csv row. It works on the interval records in `D['recs']`, which `build_facts.py` made before. Field `GBps` of a part A record is the column `aggregate_GBps` of the interval line of the csv file. The binary computes that column as the sum of the bytes of all threads divided by the longest per-thread time. It prints the column with 2 decimal places [Ref6]. Field `GBps` of a bwx record is the sum over the T rows of the interval of bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9. Each T row uses the elapsed time of its own thread. The column aggregate_GBps of the I row is not used as the rate [Ref2] [Ref3]. Two blocks use parsed values that are not records. The block on hardware error records (lines 241 to 439) uses the interval dicts of `D['hw']` and `D['hw_cmp']`, with the rate in the field `total`. Line 512 and lines 1550 to 1552 print values of these dicts again. The check of the estimate (lines 844 to 851) uses the `thread` lines of A1.csv and the column per_thread_avg_GBps of its interval lines [Ref2].

Rows that are left out before this file runs. From rows L-2, L-3, L-4, R0, R0b, X1d10, X1d10b and BASEd10 only oldread at position 0 and asmread at position 1 are records. From the folders of runner bwx only the kernels oldread, read and asmread are records, and only the processes whose tag starts with `common-6000-`, `b5-fwd-` or `b5-rev-`. From A3.csv only the processes with the tags onebuf-ms500-1, onebuf-ms500-2 and onebuf-ms500-3 are records [Ref3]. From a run folder of an earlier bwx12 or bwx11 row only the csv files that the row list of `build_facts.py` names give records. Example: the folder of row L-1 holds 5 csv files, and only a6456.csv gives records. From the folder partA-20261113T205055Z only A1.csv and A3.csv give records [Ref3]. A part A csv file also holds one `best` line per process and kernel, with the highest aggregate_GBps of its intervals. The parser skips this line. So it is not a record [Ref2] [Ref6].

How records are selected here. `sel(recs, field=value, ...)` returns the records that match every condition. A condition value may be one value, a set of values or a function. Example: `sel(recs, dataset=set(BW12), kernel='asmread', pos=1)` returns asmread at position 1 of rows L-1 to L-4 [Ref2].

Statistics. The file takes no mean over the intervals of a list. A list of intervals is described by `rng`: lowest value, highest value, median, number of intervals, number of processes, number of sessions and number of boots. `med` is the median of `GBps` of a list. For an even number of values the median is the mean of the two middle values [Ref1] [Ref2].

The test of rule V1 point 2. `compare(r72, r80)` forms the range `a` of the 7200 MT/s records and the range `b` of the 8000 MT/s records. `overlap` is true when `a.lo <= b.hi` and `b.lo <= a.hi`. `dist` is the distance of the nearest ends in GB/s. It is positive when the 7200 MT/s range lies above, negative when it lies below, and 0 when the ranges overlap. `wording` is "no difference seen" for an overlap and "differs between the 8000 MT/s boot and the 7200 MT/s boot" otherwise. `width` is (b.hi - b.lo) / b.lo x 100, in percent [Ref1] [Ref2].

Which test decides. `cmps` tests each 7200 MT/s row against one or more 8000 MT/s scopes. Only a scope with `decides` = True gets a wording. It is the pool A-1 to A-3 for `bw_old read` of part A, and the pool L-1 to L-4 for the bwx12 rows. The other scopes are printed without a wording. Six part C rows have no deciding test. Three of them are tested against the pool L-1 to L-4 with `decides` = False: oldread of cfwd at position 0, asmread as first interval, and asmread after read. The other three are tested only against rows of runner bwx, also with `decides` = False: oldread of crev at position 2, read after oldread, and read after asmread. So part C gets two wordings: one for all its oldread intervals and one for asmread after oldread.

Rule V3 rows (part A, load-only kernels) do not use `compare`. `facts_text.py` counts how many of the 3 intervals of session 1 lie above, below or inside the 8000 MT/s range of the same round (`pa3`). Sessions 2 and 3 of part A are not part of this test. Rule V3 uses them for Q1 only [Ref5]. Lines 723 to 733 turn the counts into the wording "inside" or "outside". A cell with mixed counts gets a text with the three counts. No percent is computed [Ref1].

Rounding. `g` prints a rate with 2 decimal places. `pc` prints a percent value with 1 decimal place. Both round half up. Range tests, differences and medians use the values before rounding. One check compares rounded text: line 199 prints the oldread rates of the three 10-module rows with `%.1f` and searches this text in the DIMM report. The columns "Distance of the nearest ends" of the test tables use the Python format `%+.2f` and not `g` (lines 85, 796 and 833). The estimate column of line 833 uses `%+.1f`. The other number columns of the table of thread rates (lines 832 and 833) and the two differences of lines 858 and 860 use `%.2f` or `%.1f`. These formats round the binary value of the number. So they can differ from `g` by one step for a value that ends in 5 at the next decimal place (tested: 2.675 gives `2.67` with `%.2f` and `2.68` with `g`). Values for `facts.json` are rounded with the Python function `round` in lines 742, 1387, 1388, 1432 and 1433. Later `build_facts.py` rounds every decimal number of `V` and of the interval records to 3 decimal places when it writes `facts.json` [Ref1] [Ref3].

`need(condition, text)` stops the whole build with an error message when the condition is false. The file holds 89 calls of `need`. Most calls guard one sentence of the sheet: the build only finishes when the data show the pattern that the sentence states. A few calls guard a table or a later step, for example the calls in lines 53 and 848. A `need` line computes no rate [Ref1].

What the function changes. `section4` returns nothing. It appends Markdown lines to the list `L`. It adds entries to the verdict object `V`. It stores values in the context `c` under the keys `hw`, `oldL`, `byst`, `partC_view`, `byst_other`, `thr`, `kF1`, `kI1`, `kAao`, `Aao`, `dist`, `mesh` and `f72_limit`. After the call, `facts_text.py` builds section 0 (the short version) from these values [Ref1].

Verdicts written to `V`: `q2_rows` (one entry per range test), `q2_old_read`, `q2_new_read`, their join `q2`, `same_boot`, `pool_8000_by_start_state`, `part_A_thread_rates`, `insufficient_data` and `hypotheses`. `build_facts.py` writes `V` to `facts.json` under the key "verdicts" [Ref3].
Sections of FACTS.md written by this file: 4.1 to 4.9 (Q2), 5 (record-only table of part A) and 6 (established, not established, hypotheses) [Ref4].

Q1 is not computed here. The percent drop of the new read kernel against the old read kernel comes from `facts_text.py`. Section 6 of this file only prints these values: `c['dl']`, `c['di']`, `c['df']` and the second element of each `CG` entry [Ref1].

Views that are not part of the rules fixed before the run: the comparison of intervals with hardware error records (section 4.1), the pool split by start state (section 4.2), the view at an equal pass count and the estimate from 120 x the per-thread average (section 4.3), and the sums per mesh (section 4.7). The rules file holds none of these five views [Ref5]. The text templates of this file say that the views of sections 4.1, 4.2 and 4.7 were added or looked at after the numbers were seen. They say that the view at an equal pass count was added while the sheet was built. They do not say when the estimate was added. Section 2 of FACTS.md says it. By its decision (o) the view at an equal pass count and the table of thread rates were added after the numbers were seen. `facts_text.py` writes that section [Ref1] [Ref4]. None of the five views calls `cmps` or `q2row`. So none of them adds a wording by rule V1 point 2.

Thresholds that this file sets. `LIM` = 1.0 GB/s (line 353): a difference between the two rounds of a process counts only above this value. Load 1.0 (lines 533 and 534): a process launched at a 1-minute load average below 1.0 belongs to the group `idle`, every other process to the group `busy`. 30 s (lines 537, 569 and 593): the longest time between the end of a 120-thread process and a launch that counts as a start after 120-thread work. `full` = 64 x 6 + 56 x 5 = 664 passes (line 777). `half` = 120 x 0.005 = 0.6 GB/s (line 819), the largest rounding error of 120 x a value that is rounded to 0.01 GB/s. More fixed limits are used in `need` lines only: 60 s after 120-thread work and a 5-minute load average of 1.0 for control I (lines 898 and 899), 10 %CPU and 1 %CPU in the process lists (lines 1081 and 1307), 1 % for the old read kernel (lines 491 and 1204), and load 1 inside row L-2 (line 1563). Two more such limits: 1.2 GB/s (2 x `half`) for the estimate from 120 x average (lines 842 and 851), and 2 s after the process start for the error records of row L-1 (line 1163). They stop the build. They select no data.

Main places where rates are selected, grouped or compared. Hardware error records: lines 297 to 303 (the lowest asmread interval of the pool L-1 to L-4 and the pool without it) and 353 to 358 (differences between the two rounds). Old read kernel: lines 446 to 459 (part A), 471 to 491 (part L), 523 to 611 (start-state groups) and 670 to 701 (part C). New read kernel in part A: lines 723 to 765 (rule V3 and medians), 777 to 796 (equal pass count) and 819 to 851 (120 x average). asmread in part L: lines 881 to 893 and 916 to 920. Load-only kernels in part C: lines 945 to 964, 988 to 1016 and 1030 to 1034. Three visits: lines 1045 to 1048, 1070 to 1074 and 1146 to 1151. Highest values at 8000 MT/s in section 4.6: lines 1110 to 1131 and 1183 to 1186. 10-module rows: lines 1191 to 1206. Sums per mesh: lines 1220 to 1259. Tables kept as a record: lines 1291 to 1296 and 1443 to 1451. Round 2 above round 1 in part A: lines 1462 to 1468. Rates of hypothesis H1 from rows R0 and L-2: lines 1560 to 1563.

Formatting code. A line `w(...)` appends one line of Markdown text. A line `L.extend(table(...))` appends one table. Most lines of the file are such text templates with `%` placeholders. The values in the placeholders come from the statistics named above.
The imported names `gap` and `sess` are not called in this file.

How to read the call sequence: a helper is listed at its first call. `ranges` and `cmps` are listed at every call. Each call writes one table of the Q2 comparison. Two more entries differ. `_q` is listed at its direct call in line 627. `g` calls it before that. `q2row` is listed a second time at its direct call in line 963.

words.def: the Arm reference server under test. It has 128 CPUs.
the two halves of the chip. CPUs 0-63 sit on mesh 0. CPUs 64-127 sit on mesh 1.
our runs use CPUs 0-119 only: 64 threads on mesh 0 plus 56 threads on mesh 1. Each thread reads its own buffer of 256 MiB from memory.
million transfers per second, the unit of memory speed.
one DIMM. CRB has 12 slots.
the inner loop of the benchmark that reads memory. On this page "kernel" means this loop. The operating system kernel is always written "Linux kernel".
portable C code with 16 running sums. Each load is followed by an add. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_old and `oldread` in the runner bwx12.
NEON intrinsics (C functions that map to Arm vector instructions), loads only. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_new and `read` in bwx12.
a hand-written load-only loop. It has the same 8 "ldp q" loads per 256 B as the new read kernel. "ldp q" is the Arm instruction that loads two 16-byte vector registers.
the new read kernel or asmread.
test loops of bwx12: the asmread loop with 96 or 256 no-operation instructions per 256 B, and a loop with one load per 64 B line.
the benchmark and its two binaries of 2026-11-13. bw_old was built from the old source, bw_new from the new source.
later runner programs for the same loops. They print one row per thread. bwx12 is the runner of the 2026-11-15 investigation. bwx11 and bwx are older versions.

a process is one start of a benchmark binary. An interval is one timed measurement inside a process. bwx12 times a sequence of kernels and repeats the sequence: each repeat is a round (counted from 0), and the position is the place of a kernel in the sequence (counted from 0). In part A the round (1 or 2) is the round of the script: round 2 runs the processes in the reverse order.
one pass of go.sh through part A, part L and part C.
the 120-thread part of the test of 2026-11-13, repeated with the same two binaries.
one bwx12 process with the kernel sequence oldread, asmread, read_nop96, read_nop256, read_1pl.
one bwx12 process with the sequence oldread, read, asmread (cfwd) or asmread, read, oldread (crev).
the part L line, started from an idle machine, twice. It was added after the first numbers were seen. It is not part of the plan fixed before the run.
the arguments of one bwx12 process, as a spec file holds them. "The same line" means a process with the same arguments.
a launch at a 1-minute load average below 1.0.
one time at which the same line was run. A later visit is the same line run again at a later time.
a line that go.sh or go2.sh prints with the time, the boot id, MemTotal, the load, the logins and the processes per user.

the row kinds of a bwx csv file: one I row per interval, one T row per thread and interval, one P row per thread before the first interval and after each interval (it holds the page state of the buffer), and one C row per thread and interval with counter values.
the stop rule of bandwidth.c: after the minimum time (0.5 s here) each thread finishes the pass over its buffer that it is in. The threads stop at different times.

the stop rule of the bwx runners in the rows used here: all threads stop at the same time. The interval length (`min_ms`) is 4 s in rows L-2, L-3, L-4 and R0b. It is 6 s in every other bwx row of this file.

total_bytes / bytes_per_thread of an interval row of part A. For the kernels read and asmread this is the number of buffer passes that all 120 threads completed in the interval. The records hold it in the field `passes`.
part A: the column aggregate_GBps that bandwidth.c prints. bwx runners: the sum over the threads of bytes / elapsed time. Unit GB/s.

the load average is the number of tasks that are runnable or wait for disk input and output, averaged by Linux over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes. "Load at launch" is the 1-minute value read directly before a process starts. The code names it `load1` or `load1_at_launch`.

the column pcpu of the tool ps in the process lists of env.txt. It is the CPU time that a process has used, divided by the time since the process started. So it is an average over the life of the process.
a boot is one run of Linux from its start to its shutdown. The boot id is a random identifier that Linux creates at each start. Equal boot ids mean the same boot.

the text in the field `boot` of an 8000 MT/s record, for example `boot -5 of the DIMM report (Linux start 2026-11-09 21:20 UTC)`. It gives the boot number of the DIMM report and the start time of Linux. A 7200 MT/s record holds the boot id in this field.

fields of a record: the memory speed in MT/s, the number of memory modules and the boot. `build_facts.py` sets the three fields. It does not read them from the files of the run folder. For an 8000 MT/s row they come from the DIMM report, for the time in the name of the run folder. A record of the rerun, of control I or of F72d12 gets the memory speed, the number of DIMM sockets and the boot id of try6.txt. An integrity check of `build_facts.py` compares the boot id of every state line and of every probe.txt with the boot id of try6.txt [Ref3]. probe.txt is the file that ra.sh (the script that runs part A) writes into a part A folder. It holds the boot id, MemTotal, the load and the sha256 of the two binaries.
the usable memory that Linux reports, in kB.
the log store of Linux. It keeps the Linux kernel log of earlier boots.

a message that the firmware passes to Linux when hardware reports an error. Linux prints it in the Linux kernel log with the tag "[Hardware Error]". Its severity is "corrected" (the hardware repaired it) or "recoverable" (not repaired, the system continues). In the code one record is one journal line "Hardware error from APEI ...".
firmware settings that limit the read requests of the cores. They are not memory settings. They were changed for another investigation.
the exit status of a process. 0 means success.
a checksum. Two files with the same sha256 have the same content.
an earlier 8000 MT/s run with 12 modules that used the same binary and method as a part of the rerun. The list was fixed before the run.
earlier 8000 MT/s runs that differ in interval length or counter setup (supporting), or that used another runner binary (other binary).
the number of measurements that a range comes from. It is written as intervals / processes / sessions / boots (rule V1 point 1).
estimated, not measured directly.
1e9 bytes. GB/s is the unit of every rate.
at 7200 MT/s with 12 memory modules, is the whole-chip read rate of the new read kernel still below that of the old read kernel, and by how much.
did either kernel's rate differ from the earlier runs with 12 modules at 8000 MT/s.

(1 - rate of the load-only kernel / rate of oldread) x 100, in percent. Both intervals come from the same bwx12 process and round. `facts_text.py` computes it. `c['dl']`, `c['di']`, `c['df']` and the second element of each `CG` entry hold these values.

the run of 2026-11-17 at 7200 MT/s by the driver script go.sh: three sessions with parts A, L and C, and one more part C process. The records of these parts have a `dataset` that starts with `rerun-`. Control I was run afterwards by the second driver script go2.sh. Its records have the dataset `control-I`.
the Markdown file `S/FACTS.md` that `build_facts.py` writes. It is the source for the report of the rerun. The text templates call it "this sheet".
the file S/FACTS.md as it is now in the folder (file time 2026-11-18 04:55 UTC). Values quoted from it are examples of what the code printed with the present data [Ref4].
the second output of `build_facts.py`: every interval as one record, plus the objects "meta" and "verdicts".

folders. R is the results folder `crb/results`. S is the folder of this file, `crb/tmp/agent-scratch/w120-7200-2026-11-17`. W15 is the folder of the 2026-11-15 investigation, `crb/tmp/agent-scratch/w120-2026-11-15`.

the three argument lines of bwx12 in folder S. like.spec is the line of part L and of control I. cfwd.spec and crev.spec are the two lines of part C. The three lines differ only in the kernel sequence after `--seq`.

files that the runner script rx.sh writes into a run folder. launches.txt holds one launch line directly before a process starts (time, load averages, arguments) and one rc line after it ends (exit status, time). env.txt holds the date, the Linux release, the load, a process list and the sha256 of the binary. r0.sh is the runner script of row R0. It writes the same two files. Its env.txt holds no sha256 of the binary.

`f72la` is the launch line of the F72d12 process (tag a6456) from its launches.txt: time, load averages, arguments, and the time of the rc line. `fenv` is the parsed env.txt of the F72d12 folder: `start` (its date line), `top` (the process list as user, %CPU, command, line number) and `n_lines` (the number of lines of the file). Both are set in lines 38 and 39.

records in `R/dimm7200-20261117`. try6.txt holds the reading of 12 modules at 7200 MT/s with the boot id of the rerun. boots.txt and gaps.txt number the boots of the journal. Their row 0 is the boot of try6.txt, with its first and last time.

words.term: First Linux kernel log line of the boot
words.def: the time after `first=` in row 0 of gaps.txt, stored as `try6['first_log_utc']`. The code uses it as the start of the boot when it prints a time since boot.

the output line of the Linux command `uptime` in gaps.txt. It holds the time of day at which gaps.txt was written (`try6['gaps_uptime_utc']`). The process-list lines after it are stored as `try6['gaps_top']`.
the file `machines/arm-crb/DIMM-flaky-report.md`. It holds the boot history of CRB with the module count of each boot (`fd.DIMM_REPORT`).
the facts sheet of the investigation of 2026-11-15 into the drop of the read rate, in folder W15.

words.term: Rules V1 to V4, F1, F2
words.def: the comparison rules in `S/baselines-and-rules.txt`, written before go.sh started. V1: the overlap test of 7200 MT/s against 8000 MT/s and its wording. V2: part C is grouped by the kernel that ran directly before. V3: part A, load-only kernels, wording inside or outside, no percent. V4: the fixed list of 8000 MT/s baselines. F1: the row labels and the 8000 MT/s reference of part A. F2: the bwx12 kernel read has no 8000 MT/s run [Ref5].

decisions of the agent, listed in section 2 of FACTS.md. Decision (r): the sheet follows rules V1, V2 and V4 and compares part C with 8000 MT/s rows, although rule F2 points 2 and 3 would present part C at 7200 MT/s only. Decision (p): which processes of runner bwx serve as the reference of part C.

the dict of collected data from `build_facts.py`. Keys used here: `recs` (the interval records), `rx` (run folders written by rx.sh or r0.sh, by row name), `step` (folders of runner bwx, by row name), `base` (the part A baselines A-1 to A-3), `X` (the bwx12 processes of parts L and C and of control I), `hw` and `hw_cmp` (hardware error records), `try6` (try6.txt, boots.txt and gaps.txt), `logs` (state lines of go.sh and go2.sh), `probe13` (records of the 2026-11-13 run and the path of the saved journal), `checks` (the integrity checks).

the dict of statistics from the function `analyse` of `facts_text.py`. Used here: `N['pa']` (part A, one entry per session and round with the `bw_old read` records `old` and the `bw_new read` records `new`) and `N['pool']` (a function that returns the records of several rows for one kernel and position).
the verdict object, a dict. `build_facts.py` writes it to `facts.json` under the key "verdicts".
`L` is the list of the text lines of FACTS.md. `w` is `L.append`: it adds one line.
the context dict from the function `render` of `facts_text.py`. It holds record lists, comparisons and short texts of sections 1 to 3. `section4` also stores its own results in it.

values that `section4` stores in `c`: `c['mesh']` in line 1260, `c['dist']` in line 1152 and `c['f72_limit']` in line 1308. `c['dist']`: the six asmread distances of section 4.6. `c['mesh']`: three interval counts of section 4.7. `c['f72_limit']`: one sentence on the limit of F72d12 as an idle start.
`ref(path)` returns the label `[RefN]` of a file in the file list of section 7 of FACTS.md.
a function of `render` in `facts_text.py`. It appends one range test to `V['q2_rows']`: both ranges, both n, the overlap flag, the distance, and the wording when `decides` is true.
`need(condition, text)` stops the build with an error message when the condition is false.

one run of `build_facts.py`, which calls `render` and `section4` and writes FACTS.md and facts.json. "The build stops" means that `need` ends this run with an error message. The run then writes no FACTS.md and no facts.json.

a test that `build_facts.py` runs on the raw files and on the scripts before the text of the sheet is built. `D['checks']` holds one result per check. Line 1461 stops the build unless every check passed. Section 1.4 of the present sheet lists 27 checks, all with the result `pass` [Ref3] [Ref4]. Since 2026-11-24 a new build stops at line 1461. Check 20 (key `sha-local`) fails then. It compares the sha256 of go.sh and of five other local scripts and spec files with the lists `local.sha` and `go2.sha`. Line 20 of go.sh was edited on 2026-11-24. So go.sh no longer has the sha256 that `local.sha` lists for it. The page `go.sh.md` in `S` (the explanation of go.sh) gives the record of the edit.

one dict per interval in `D['recs']`. Fields used in this file: `dataset`, `binary`, `binary_sha256`, `kernel`, `kernel_before`, `round`, `pos`, `session`, `tag`, `proc_key`, `GBps`, `mesh0_GBps`, `mesh1_GBps`, `passes`, `per_thread_avg_GBps`, `speed_MTps`, `modules`, `boot`, `load1_at_launch`, `min_ms`, `stop`, `start`, `count`, `folder`, `file`, `line`.
field of a record: the rate of one interval in GB/s. Part A: the column `aggregate_GBps` of the csv file. bwx runners: the sum over the T rows (threads) of bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9.
fields of a bwx record: the sum of the thread rates on CPUs 0-63 and on CPUs 64-127. Their sum is `GBps`.
field of a part A record: the column of the same name in the csv file. It is the average rate of the 120 threads of the interval, rounded to 0.01 GB/s.
field of a record: one value per process. `rng` counts the processes of a list with it.

field of a bwx record: the kernel that was timed directly before in the same process. For the first interval of a process it is the text "none (first interval of the process)" (`FIRST`). `facts_data.py` takes the value from the kernel sequence in the header line `# bwx:` of the csv file (`seq=`). It does not compare the times of the intervals [Ref2]. In a part A record the field names the process before it in the csv file. This file does not read it there.
field of a bwx record: the position of the kernel in the sequence, counted from 0.

fields of a record. `min_ms`: the least length of an interval in ms (option `--min-ms`). The sheet prints it as the interval length. `stop`: the stop rule. For a part A record `build_facts.py` sets `min_ms` to the constant 500 and `stop` to the constant `whole pass`. It does not read them from the csv file. For a bwx record both values come from the header lines that the binary prints into the csv file [Ref2] [Ref3]. `start`: the value of the runner option `--start` (`common` or `offset`). `count`: 1 when the run read core counters.

the short name of a run folder or of a process. Rerun: T72A1 to T72A3 (the part A folders of sessions 1 to 3), T72L1 to T72L3 (part L), T72C1 to T72C4 (part C, T72C4 ran after the three sessions). Control I: T72I1 and T72I2. Earlier bwx12 and bwx11 folders: the name of the csv file without `.csv`, for example a6456 or p2add. Runner bwx: the tag of the `-- step` line, for example common-6000-common-p1. Rows A-2 and A-3: the tag of the `-- step` line of the process, for example onebuf-ms500-1. Row A-1 has no tag.

a header line of a csv file that starts with `-- step`. The run script writes it directly before it starts a process: run_bwx.sh for runner bwx, run_partA.sh for A1.csv and A3.csv. It holds the tag, the binary, the load averages, the time and the arguments of the process.

field `dataset` of a record names the row that the record belongs to. A row is one group of processes. Rows of the rerun: `rerun-A`, `rerun-L`, `rerun-C`. Row of control I: `control-I`. Rows of earlier runs have the names below.

the 8000 MT/s baseline rows of part A, all of 2026-11-13. A-1: `threads120.csv` of the folder kernels-20261113T181222Z, same process order as part A. A-2: `A1.csv` of the folder partA-20261113T205055Z, same binaries, other process order. The code labels its arguments as the same (line 94). The `-- step` lines of A1.csv show two differences from part A. The CPU list is written `0-63,64-119` in place of `0-119`. The option `--per-thread` is added: the binary prints one more line per thread and interval. A-3: `A3.csv` of the same folder, bw_old read only.

the bwx12 rows at 8000 MT/s. L-1 is the baseline: one process with the argument line of like.spec (folder w120-R8). L-2 to L-4 are supporting rows (folders w120-R1, w120-R5, w120-R6): 4 s intervals and other counter events.
rows of the other binary bwx11 at 8000 MT/s (folders w120-R0 and w120-R0b).
rows of the first runner bwx at 8000 MT/s: the processes with the tags `common-6000-*` in two B7 folders and two C3 folders of 2026-11-13 and 2026-11-14.

rows of runner bwx from two B5 folders of 2026-11-14. Rows B5a and B5b hold the processes with the tags `b5-fwd-*`. Rows B5a-rev and B5b-rev hold the processes with the tags `b5-rev-*`, which ran the kernels in the reverse order.

a 12-module run with a firmware test setting. It is shown and not used as a baseline. One check also uses its two oldread intervals. Line 607 tests that the highest oldread rate of part L lies below every oldread record at 8000 MT/s with 12 modules (list `allo`, line 604).

runs in boots with 10 memory modules. The row table of section 4.1 lists them. Lines 197 to 201 compare their oldread rates with the DIMM report. Lines 1191 to 1210 use them for the texts of rule V1 points 3 and 4. No range test uses them.
one bwx12 process with the argument line of like.spec, run in the boot of the rerun at 7200 MT/s, before the rerun. It is a sample of the same boot. It is not a baseline and not part of the rerun.

the intervals of several rows taken together as one list. Each pool holds the intervals of one kernel. Example: "pool L-1 to L-4" for oldread is `P12o`, every oldread interval at position 0 of rows L-1, L-2, L-3 and L-4.

`A72o`: `bw_old read` of part A. `A80o`: `bw_old read` of rows A-1 to A-3. `L72o`, `L72a`: oldread and asmread of part L. `I72o`, `I72a`: the same of control I. `F72o`, `F72a`: the same of row F72d12. `C72o`: oldread of part C. `P12o`, `P12a`: oldread at position 0 and asmread at position 1 of rows L-1 to L-4. `PALLo`, `PALLa`: the same with rows R0 and R0b added. In these names 72 stands for 7200 MT/s, 80 for 8000 MT/s, o for the old read kernel and a for asmread.

the dict that `rng` returns for a list of records: `lo` (lowest value), `hi` (highest value), `med` (median), `n` (number of intervals), `procs` (number of processes), `sessions` and `boots`. The value is `GBps` unless another field is named.
the middle value of a sorted list (Python `statistics.median`). For an even number of values it is the mean of the two middle values.
the rounding rule of `g`, `sp`, `pc` and `_q`: a value exactly between two steps is rounded away from zero. `_q` rounds the value to 6 decimal places before it applies the rule.
the dict that `compare(r72, r80)` returns: `a` (range of the 7200 MT/s records), `b` (range of the 8000 MT/s records), `overlap`, `dist`, `wording` and `width`.

`cLo`, `cLa`: part L against the pool L-1 to L-4, for oldread and for asmread. `cIo`, `cIa`: control I against the same pool. `cFo`, `cFa`: F72d12 against the same pool. `cAo`: `A72o` against `A80o`. `cCo`: `C72o` against `P12o`.
two min-to-max ranges share at least one value.

for two ranges that do not overlap: the lowest value of the higher range minus the highest value of the lower range, in GB/s. In the code the sign is positive when the first range given to `compare` is the higher one. In a test against 8000 MT/s the first range is the 7200 MT/s range. The value is 0 when the ranges overlap.
for two ranges: the highest value of the higher range minus the lowest value of the lower range, in GB/s. In the code: `far` (line 489), `far_boot` and `far_pool` (line 1148).
the width of a range in percent of its lower end: (hi - lo) / lo x 100. For an 8000 MT/s range, rule V1 point 2 calls it the size that the test cannot exclude.
the fixed text that rule V1 point 2 gives to a test. `SAME` = "no difference seen" when the ranges overlap. `DIFFERS` = "differs between the 8000 MT/s boot and the 7200 MT/s boot" when they do not.

in `cmps`, a scope is one 8000 MT/s record list that a 7200 MT/s row is tested against, for example "L-1 alone" or "pool L-1 to L-4". `decides` is a flag of the scope. True: the wording of this test is the result of the row. False: the test is printed without a wording.
the range test of a 7200 MT/s row against the scope that has `decides` = True. Only this test gets a wording by rule V1 point 2.

`pa3` is a list of 6 cells from `facts_text.py` for rule V3: bw_new read, bw_new asmread and bw_old asmread, each in round 1 and round 2. A cell holds the 3 intervals of session 1 (`s1`), the 3 intervals of row A-1 (`a1`) and the intervals of row A-2 (`a2`: 3 intervals, or none for bw_old asmread). `b80` is the 8000 MT/s range of the round: the range of the intervals of `a1` and `a2` together. The cell also holds the distances of the session-1 intervals that lie above this range (`above`) or below it (`below`), and the number that lie inside it (`inside`). `newread` holds the two cells of bw_new read.

the load-only intervals of part C in five groups, by the kernel that ran directly before (rule V2): read after oldread, read after asmread, asmread after read, asmread first, asmread after oldread. Each entry is a pair: the records, and their percent drops against oldread of the same process and round.

a dict by tag of the steps that go.sh and go2.sh ran: one entry per part A folder and one per bwx12 process. Fields used here: `part` (A, L, C or I), `tag`, `state` (text of the start state), `gap_s` (seconds between the end of the entry before and this launch), `load1` (load at launch), `first` (launch time, for part A of its first process), `prev` (the entry before).
what the machine did before a launch. The code describes it by the load at launch and by the time since the previous 120-thread process ended.

the two start-state groups of the processes of rows L-1 to L-4 (lines 533 and 534). `idle`: launched at a 1-minute load average below 1.0. `busy`: every other process. The checks in lines 536 to 538 show that each `busy` process was launched at most 30 s after a process with `--threads 120` ended.

record lists of the start-state view (line 540). `Io`, `Bo`: oldread at position 0 of the groups `idle` and `busy`. `Ia`, `Ba`: asmread at position 1 of the two groups. `aIo`, `aBo`, `aIa`, `aBa` are their ranges.
the time from the launch line to the rc line of the process in launches.txt. Both lines give whole seconds.

the three positions of a hardware error record against an interval (`kind`). The journal and launches.txt give whole seconds. So the code gives a record a span of 2 s: from N - 1 to N + 1 seconds after the process start, where N is the journal time minus the time of the launch line. Inside: the whole span lies in the interval. Possible: the span and the interval share a part. The text prints it as "before or inside". Outside: neither.
in the block on hardware error records: the intervals that the sheet uses, oldread at position 0 and asmread at position 1, in each round of a process.
the interval of the same kernel at the same position in the other round of the same process. The processes of this comparison have two rounds, 0 and 1.

`D['hw']` holds one entry per process of rows L-1 to L-4, R0 and R0b with the error records in its window. `D['hw_cmp']` holds three lists. `rows`: intervals to which records can be assigned. `border`: records at the border of two intervals. `clean`: positions of the processes with records at which neither round has a record inside it or at its border.

field of an entry of `D['hw_cmp']`, in GB/s. In `rows` and in the `intervals` of a `border` entry it is the rate of the interval minus the rate of its other round. In `clean` it is the rate of round 1 minus the rate of round 0.
field of an interval of a bwx csv file, as `D['hw']` and `D['hw_cmp']` hold it: the sum over its T rows of bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9, in GB/s. The interval record holds the same value as `GBps`.
two values of the runner option `--start`. This file does not say what the option does. It only keeps the processes of the two values apart (`scm`).
an estimate (est.) of the sum of the thread rates of a part A interval: 120 threads times `per_thread_avg_GBps`. The column is rounded to 0.01 GB/s. So the estimate is exact to 0.6 GB/s.

constants from `facts_text.py` that the templates insert. `ADDED` = "added after the first numbers were seen". `NOT_PLAN` = "not part of the plan fixed before the run". `NO_READ` = "Insufficient data: no 8000 MT/s run of kernel read with bwx12". `STANDIN` says that asmread is used in place of the new read kernel. `F2_NOTE` names decision (r). `H1_MEAS` names the measurement of hypothesis H1. Two more constants are set in this file (lines 14 and 15). `OWN` ends the table label of the rows F72d12 and control I. `OLD_OWN` ends their key in `facts.json`.
the words of a `w(...)` line or of another text template that are written as they stand in the code. No value from the data is inserted into them.
a text template without a placeholder for a measured value. The code prints it unchanged, or with a fixed label such as `ADDED`.
the five hypotheses of section 6: start state, time since boot, memory speed, pass counts in part A, load values. None of them is tested.

functions.name: secs
functions.what: Returns the interval lengths of a record list as text, for example `6 s`, from the field `min_ms`.

functions.name: section4
functions.what: Writes sections 4, 5 and 6 of FACTS.md, runs the Q2 range tests, and stores the Q2 verdicts and the hypotheses in `V`.

functions.name: one_v
functions.what: Lambda. Prints the one rate of a list with one record, or the lowest-to-highest range of a longer list.

functions.name: src
functions.what: Returns the `[RefN]` labels of the csv files that hold the given records, each file once.

functions.name: ranges
functions.what: Builds a range table: one row per record list with memory speed, modules, n, lowest to highest rate, median and source files.

functions.name: source
functions.what: Builds the Source cell of the section 4.1 row table: csv files, plus the files with the load and the binary sha256.

functions.name: cmps
functions.what: Runs `compare` for each 7200 MT/s row against each 8000 MT/s scope, stores each test with `q2row`, and returns the overlap table.

functions.name: noseq
functions.what: Lambda. Removes the value of `--seq` from an argument line. The lines can then be compared without the kernel sequence.

functions.name: kind_txt
functions.what: Returns the position of one error record as text: `outside`, `inside` plus the interval, or `before or inside` plus the interval.

functions.name: sg
functions.what: Lambda. Prints a difference in GB/s with 2 decimal places and its sign. A value that rounds to zero prints as `0.00`.

functions.name: c['hw']['cmp']['lst']
functions.what: Lambda. Stored in `c`. Joins a list of texts with commas, and with `and` before the last text.

functions.name: lst
functions.what: Lambda. Joins a list of texts with commas, and with `and` before the last text.

functions.name: lrows
functions.what: Lambda. Returns one range-table row per row L-1 to L-4, for the given kernel and position.

functions.name: orows
functions.what: Lambda. Returns one range-table row per row R0 and R0b, for the given kernel and position.

functions.name: grp
functions.what: Lambda. Returns the records of rows L-1 to L-4 for one kernel and position whose process is in the given start-state group.

functions.name: loads
functions.what: Lambda. Returns the sorted loads at launch of the given processes.

functions.name: names
functions.what: Lambda. Returns the given processes as text: row name and tag, joined with commas.

functions.name: lsrc
functions.what: Lambda. Returns the `[RefN]` labels of the launches.txt files of the given processes, each file once.

functions.name: scm
functions.what: Lambda. Keeps the records whose process ran with `--start common`.

functions.name: cellt
functions.what: Lambda. Prints the intervals of one cell as rate and pass count in brackets, or `no process in this row` for an empty list.

functions.name: same
functions.what: Lambda. Keeps the records with 663 or 664 passes (`full - 1` or `full`).

functions.name: av
functions.what: Lambda. Returns the values of the field `per_thread_avg_GBps` of a record list. Line 1046 reuses the name for a range.

functions.name: span
functions.what: Lambda. Prints a list of numbers as one value when all are equal, otherwise as lowest to highest.

functions.name: m_k
functions.what: Lambda. Returns a pair for a scope that matches in the kernel before: the key in facts.json and the label in the table.

functions.name: in_
functions.what: Lambda. True when a value lies inside a range, the two ends included.

functions.name: where
functions.what: Lambda. Describes one record as text: process tag, folder, position, kernel before and the line of its I row.

functions.name: mrow
functions.what: Returns one table row of section 4.7: label, memory speed, interval count, range of the mesh 0 sums, range of the mesh 1 sums, source.

functions.name: side
functions.what: Lambda. Prints both sides of a comparison for a verdict: range and n at 7200 MT/s, range and n at 8000 MT/s.

functions.name: sgn
functions.what: Lambda. The same as `sg`: prints a difference in GB/s with its sign.

refs.what: Defines `need`, `_q`, `g`, `sp`, `pc`, `pcr`, `nn`, `nns`, `table` and the fixed texts (lines 18 to 137), `med` and `analyse` with `pool` (lines 279 to 330) and `compare` (lines 333 to 336). Its function `render` defines `q2row` (lines 359 to 368), prepares the record lists, the comparisons and `pa3` (lines 413 to 439), calls `section4` (lines 1458 to 1464) and then builds section 0 from `c` (line 1467).

Defines `sel`, `rng`, `overlap`, `gap` and `width_pct` (lines 442 to 485). Its parsers compute the rate of an interval: `read_k120` takes the column aggregate_GBps of a part A csv file (lines 264 to 304), and `bwx_intervals` sums bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9 over the T rows of a bwx csv file (lines 356 to 383). Places the hardware error records with `hw_records` and `hw_compare` (lines 293 to 397). The function `run_checks` (lines 653 to 894) holds the integrity checks. `main` is in lines 1033 to 1052. It calls `run_checks` before `render`.

The output file. Sections 4, 5 and 6 are lines 436 to 949. The word list is lines 38 to 89. Lines 95 and 96 define Q1 and Q2. Section 2 (lines 275 to 302) lists the decisions (a) to (r). Section 1.4 (lines 211 to 239) lists the integrity checks.
